title: Small Space Heaters for One Chilly Room: Safety Features, Running Costs and Where Not to Put One
subtitle: A plain-English guide to the shut-offs that matter, what a heater adds to your electric bill and the placement rules that help keep a room warm and safe.
excerpt: A small plug-in heater can take the chill off a den or bedroom. Here is what the safety features do, what one costs to run and why safety shut-offs are only a backup to good placement.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: Many homes have one room that never quite warms up. It might be the den where you read in the evening, a sewing room over the garage or a back bedroom at the end of the hall. Turning up the whole-house thermostat for one room can feel wasteful, and a sweater only goes so far.

A small plug-in space heater can help. It is also an appliance that deserves respect. The Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) estimates that portable heaters, including electric ones, were involved in an average of 1,600 fires a year from 2020 to 2022, with about 70 deaths and 150 injuries a year. That is why where you put a heater, and how you use it, matters so much.
How a small space heater works

The heaters in this guide are ceramic heaters, meaning they use a ceramic heating element. The Lasko models below list 1,500 watts on high, and the MyHeat Max also has a 900-watt low setting. The Honeywell's product page answers a shopper question with 1,500 watts as well.

Two safety features matter most. A tip-over switch shuts the heater off if it gets knocked over. Overheat protection shuts it off if the inside gets too hot. In Consumer Reports' tip-over test, a heater earns a perfect score if it shuts off within 10 seconds of being tilted onto its face. One caution: a safety listing mark on the box does not by itself promise a tip-over switch, so look for the words "tip-over switch" or "tip-over protection" in the maker's description.

Electricity is sold by the kilowatt-hour, or kWh, which is 1,000 watts used for one hour. A heater on 1,500 watts uses 1.5 kWh an hour. As an example only, at 15 cents per kWh that works out to about 22.5 cents an hour, or roughly $27 a month if you run it four hours a day on high. This is our own arithmetic, not a published figure. A 900-watt low setting would cost about 13.5 cents an hour at that same example rate. Your bill shows your own price per kWh. Consumer Reports says most heaters in its ratings cost about $19 a month to run at a national average rate, and notes that a space heater will not necessarily lower your overall heating bill.

Shut-off switches are backups, not a substitute for good placement. Keep a heater at least 3 feet from beds, bedding, curtains and furniture, and never place one near a sleeping person. Keep it away from bathtubs, sinks and wet floors. A heater can burn someone who touches it, so keep it out of reach of children and pets. And do not share its outlet with another appliance.
"Plug electric space heaters directly into a wall outlet—never into an extension cord or power strip." — U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission

items: Tip-over switch and overheat protection, named plainly in the product description.
A cool-touch housing, so a brush of the hand is less likely to hurt.
Floor-level use if you can manage it. Consumer Reports favors floor placement, which can be harder for someone who has trouble bending or who has pets or children nearby.
A remote control. Consumer Reports suggests one so you can keep the heater on the floor and avoid kneeling to turn dials.
A thermostat or eco mode, if the product page lists one.
A timer for when you step out of the room.
Room size. Coverage is usually listed in square feet. Consumer Reports found lower-wattage personal heaters often underperformed.
The warranty, if the page lists one. Both Lasko pages below do.

Price and stock. Consumer Reports says its tested models cost $18 to $500, and nearly half of the top-rated ones cost $75 or less. Pages we looked at showed no monthly fee for the Lasko heaters; check the seller's page for the Honeywell, along with return terms and setup help.

sections.content: Setting it up and using it well
Pick a spot with that 3-foot clear zone all around. Plug it straight into a wall outlet that nothing else is using, with no extension cord or power strip.

Start on the low setting or eco mode, if your heater has one, and see whether that is enough. Use the timer to turn the heater off when you leave the room, and switch it off before bed. If you are helping a parent set one up, walk through the remote and buttons together.
Consumer Reports puts it simply: "Don't rely on the timer to turn off the space heater while you sleep." The CPSC also says to turn heaters off when sleeping.
sections.label: Good to Know

sections.content: A small heater, used with a little care, can make that one cold room a pleasant place to spend an evening again. Choose one with the right safety features, give it room to breathe, and turn it off when you turn in. If a room stays cold or you feel cold often, mention it to your doctor. Stay warm out there.

products.name: Lasko MyHeat Max 9" Digital Ceramic Space Heater (CD09101, black)
products.price: $39.99 (list price, November 2026); the black version showed as unavailable, so check stock
products.blurb: A compact desk or tabletop heater listed for about 100 sq ft, with 1500 W and 900 W settings, a tip-over switch, a thermostat with Auto Eco mode, a 12-hour timer and a 3-year warranty. It has no remote, and Consumer Reports' preference for floor placement means a tabletop unit may be less suitable with pets or children nearby.

products.name: Lasko Ellipse 12" Ceramic Space Heater (CD12950, oscillating, with remote)
products.price: $69.99 (list price, November 2026); both colors showed as unavailable, so check stock
products.blurb: Listed for a room up to about 200 sq ft, and suits anyone who would rather not bend to the controls, since it includes a remote. It has a tip-over switch, child lock, eco mode, a 12-hour timer and a 3-year limited warranty. The page is inconsistent: it says "tool-free assembly" in one place and "simple base assembly required" in another, and calls the heater both a tabletop and a tower model, so confirm both with Lasko before buying.

products.name: Honeywell ThermaWave 6 Ceramic Heater (black, HCE870W)
products.price: $90.99 (Best Buy listing, October 2026); check current price
products.blurb: Listed for about 200 sq ft, with auto shut-off, a tip-over safety switch, a timer and 1500 W per the page's Q&A. A customer summary notes no fan noise and calls the price "a little pricey." It is not app-controlled, and the notes describe it as a tabletop unit.

products.name: Cozy Cove Pro Portable Heater
products.blurb: A lightweight plug-in heater with a remote and an adjustable thermostat, meant for warming one room rather than a whole house. The seller describes it as quiet and needing no installation.
